title: Valiant-for-Truth crosses the river
hook: at the end of Pilgrim's Progress, Valiant-for-Truth crosses the river and all the trumpets sound
carry: death is a crossing, with a welcome beyond
tomorrow: he went to a meeting unwillingly. what happened at a quarter to nine?

segments.voice: Yesterday a man named Help reached into the Slough of Despond: help pulled him out. Today the same book, at the far end of the road. It's about a death, told gently.
screen: `HELP PULLED HIM OUT.` → `THE FAR END OF THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Airport arrivals: the balloons, the hand-lettered signs, somebody running before the doors fully open. A homecoming is loud. So why does a book about a long, hard walk end with trumpets? John Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress closes at a river, and the river is death. You'd expect a hush. Instead, there's a puzzle in the last scene: a man hands over his sword, keeps his scars, walks into the water, and the far bank erupts.
screen: `ARRIVALS: BALLOONS AND SIGNS.` → `A RIVER, AND IT'S DEATH.` → `HE GIVES THE SWORD, KEEPS THE SCARS.`

segments.voice: The man is Mr. Valiant-for-Truth, a pilgrim who has fought hard all the way. When word comes that it's his time, he gives his things away. "My sword I give to him that shall succeed me in my pilgrimage." That's the first half of the puzzle: the sword is a tool, and tools go to the next traveler. Then: "My marks and scars I carry with me." Why keep those? Because, he says, they're a witness that he fought the battles of the one who will now reward him. The scars aren't something to hide on arrival. They're his story, and he brings it. Then friends walk him to the riverside. As he goes in he says, "Death, where is thy sting?" and as the water rises, "Grave, where is thy victory?" Those are Paul's words, from his letter to the Corinthians. And then the line Bunyan's readers waited for: "So he passed over, and all the trumpets sounded for him on the other side." So the puzzle solves this way. Bunyan doesn't end the road at a grave. He ends it at an arrival, and on the far bank somebody has been waiting, trumpets ready.
screen: `MY SWORD I GIVE.` · `MY MARKS AND SCARS I CARRY.` · `DEATH, WHERE IS THY STING?` · `ALL THE TRUMPETS SOUNDED.` · then, large: `THE TRUMPETS SOUNDED.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and remember one real welcome: a door opening, your name called out, someone who couldn't wait for you to get there. Stay inside that moment and let the sound of it fill the room. If you pray, you can let it stand for the far bank in Bunyan's story.
The trumpets sounded. Bunyan's last scene: a river crossed, scars kept, and a welcome on the other side.
Your line: death is a crossing, with a welcome beyond. In Bunyan, the road ends at an arrival, not a grave. Day 1661, home.

howItsDone: Valiant-for-Truth's farewell is sometimes read at Christian funerals; many churches sing hymns of hope, not only sorrow, as a coffin leaves.

fork.setup: at your great-aunt's funeral, the family asks the band for something joyful as they leave. your cousin whispers that it's disrespectful. what's in Bunyan's ending?
options: trumpets on the far bank: a death told as a welcome home.
silence: Bunyan has the dead mourned without any music.
a stern warning to the living, and no celebration.
fork.reveal: friends walk Valiant to the river, he crosses, and all the trumpets sound for him on the other side. grief and welcome share the scene.

original.note: Greek: sting, goad. Paul's word in 1 Corinthians 15:55, the question Valiant asks at the river.

what a scholar hears: Valiant's words at the water are 1 Corinthians 15:55, and the scars echo Paul's 'marks of the Lord Jesus' in Galatians 6:17.

chat.says: Pop keeps saying 'when i cross the river' like it's nothing. i hate it. why is he so calm?
options: In Bunyan, pilgrims cross a river to trumpets on the far side. Pop may picture that.
He's in denial. Nobody is calm about dying unless they've given up.
Christians aren't supposed to feel sad about death, so don't let it get to you.
chat.meaning: In The Pilgrim's Progress the river is death, and all the trumpets sound on the other side. Pop's calm and Grace's sadness can both be there.

tie.story: In The Pilgrim's Progress, Valiant-for-Truth walks into the river of death saying, Death, where is thy sting? and all the trumpets sound for him on the other side.
tie.friend: Grace's Pop may picture death as that crossing, with a welcome waiting; his calm and her sadness can both be true.
tie.you: Who would you picture welcomed home on the far bank?
